def: The revelation God gave Jesus. Always singular in the Qur'an; not the four Gospels.
The revelation given to Moses. Singular in the Qur'an; not a multi-book canon.
The revelation given to David, usually understood as the Psalms {Q 4:163}.
Scrolls. The Qur'an speaks of the scrolls of Abraham and Moses {Q 87:19}.
One who attests the truth of what came before. Used of the Qur'an, and of Jesus confirming the Torah.
Confirmation: declaring true, verifying, putting right. Applied to a message or a prophet, not to a manuscript.
Guardian, witness, trusted arbiter. The Qur'an's description of itself over the earlier books {Q 5:48}.
Criterion, that which separates truth from falsehood. Applied to the Qur'an and also to the revelation given to Moses.
The People of the Book: Jews and Christians, addressed in the Qur'an.
The disciples of Jesus, who declared themselves helpers in God's cause {Q 3:52}.
A verse of the Qur'an; also a sign.
A chapter of the Qur'an. There are 114.
The recognised readings of the Qur'an, each traced to the Prophet, differing in vowels, dots and a few words.
The modes in which the Qur'an was revealed, allowing recitation in more than one form.
A bound copy of the Qur'an.
The standard copy made under ʿUthmān around 650 CE, from which copies were sent to the major cities.
A report of the words or actions of the Prophet, preserved through a chain of narrators.
The chain of narrators by which a hadith is transmitted.
Sound: the highest grade for a hadith. Also the title of the collections of al-Bukhārī and Muslim.
Good: a grade just below sound.
Weak: a hadith with a defect in its chain or text.
Stoning, the penalty for adultery in the Torah and in the hadith about the Jews of Medina.
Commentary on the Qur'an. Major works include al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr and al-Rāzī.
Transmission by so many that collusion is impossible. The basis of the Qur'an's certain text.
Distortion. Classically divided into distortion of wording (*lafẓ*) and of meaning (*maʿnā*).
Distortion of the wording of a text.
Distortion of the meaning, by misreading or explaining away.
The standard Hebrew text, fixed by Jewish scholars between about the 7th and 10th centuries.
The Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, begun in the 3rd century BCE.
The Syriac Bible. Its New Testament has 22 books.
Tatian's single Gospel woven from the four, c. 170 CE, used in the Syriac churches for centuries.
The 'three witnesses in heaven' of 1 John 5:7, absent from the early Greek manuscripts.
The story of the woman taken in adultery, John 7:53–8:11, absent from the earliest manuscripts.
The study of manuscripts to work out what an original text said.
The list of books a community accepts as scripture.
Writing under another person's name. Most scholars think several letters in Paul's name are pseudepigraphic.
The oneness of God: the centre of Islam.
The testimony of faith: 'There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God.'
A prophet. Muslims hold there was none between Jesus and Muhammad.
A messenger: a prophet who brings a scripture.
The natural disposition God places in every human to know Him.
The primordial religion of pure monotheism, taught by every prophet {Q 30:30}.
The Christian doctrine, formulated in the fourth century, that God is three persons in one being. The Qur'an rejects it {Q 4:171}.
The Christian doctrine that Christ's death pays for the sins of others. The Qur'an teaches that no soul bears another's burden {Q 53:38}.
